title: Solve Subject–Verb Agreement with the Odd-One-Out Trick
description: Use the he-or-they test to recognize a singular-versus-plural verb pattern, choose the one answer that differs from the other three, and avoid using the shortcut on verb-tense questions.

blocks.html:
A faster way to solve subject–verb agreement

The move: Test each choice after he and after they. The odd one out is the answer.

Why it pays: You answer without finding the subject or untangling the sentence — which is exactly where the test hides its interrupting phrases.

One caution: This is a shortcut with a gate. If the four choices differ in tense rather than in singular versus plural, close it and read the sentence.

Some verb questions never make you find the subject. Put each choice after he and after they: when three choices go one way and one goes the other, the odd one out is the answer — and the interrupting phrase the test buried in the sentence never mattered.

The safety rule matters: use the trick only when every answer fits exactly one of he or they.

Try the test before learning the rule

Look only at these four answer choices:

  1. is studying
  2. study
  3. have studied
  4. are studying

Put he before each choice. Then put they before each choice. Which answer behaves differently from the other three?

content.prompt: Which answer behaves differently after he and they?
content.hint: Say each full phrase aloud after he, then after they. Three fit they; one fits he.
content.explanation: Right. He is studying works, while they study, they have studied, and they are studying work. The first answer is the singular odd one out.

blocks.html:
The odd-one-out pattern

The SAT repeatedly builds subject–verb agreement questions with a visible answer pattern:

  • three choices are definitely plural and one is definitely singular, or
  • three choices are definitely singular and one is definitely plural.

The one that differs is the correct answer.

In our review of released digital SAT and earlier SAT forms, this pattern has held in every question where the safety conditions are met.

Strong students should use it too

This is not a backup for students who do not know grammar. It is faster than searching a complicated sentence for its subject, and it avoids traps built around nearby nouns.

Your job is not to explain the sentence. Your job is to verify the answer pattern.

Use he and they as testing frames

For each complete verb choice, try both frames:

  • He ___ tests whether the choice is singular.
  • They ___ tests whether the choice is plural.

For example, he inspires works but they inspires does not. So inspires is singular. They inspire works but he inspire does not. So inspire is plural.

content.prompt: Which phrase fits after they but not after he?
content.hint: Say the full phrase after they. Then check whether it also works after he.
content.explanation: Correct. They inspire works, but he inspire does not. The other three choices fit after he.

blocks.html:
Test the whole verb phrase

An answer may contain more than one word. Keep the words together:

  • he has discovered → singular
  • they have discovered → plural
  • he is discovering → singular
  • they are discovering → plural

You do not need to name the tense. Just test the entire answer.

content.prompt: How should you classify have transformed?
choices: Singular, because the phrase he have transformed sounds correct.
Neither, because the choice contains two separate words.
Both singular and plural, depending on the sentence around it.
Plural, because they have transformed works and he have transformed does not.
content.hint: Try the complete phrase after both testing words.
content.explanation: Exactly. They have transformed works; he have transformed does not. The phrase is plural.

blocks.html:
The trick has an eligibility gate

Before choosing the odd answer, verify all three conditions:

  1. All four choices are complete verb choices or verb phrases.
  2. Each choice fits he or they, but not both.
  3. The split is three to one: one singular and three plural, or three singular and one plural.

If any condition fails, stop. It is not this pattern.

content.prompt: Which answer set is safe for the odd-one-out trick?
choices: develops; develop; are developing; have developed
is developing; are developing; has developed; have developed
content.hint: Every choice must fit exactly one of he or they, and the final split must be three to one.
content.explanation: Right. Develops fits he; the other three fit they. In the second set, developed fits both. In the third, developing fits neither. The fourth set splits two and two.

blocks.html:
Run the same four steps

  1. Scan the choices. Confirm that all four are verb choices.
  2. Test he and they. Classify every choice as singular or plural.
  3. Check the gate. Every choice must fit exactly one frame, and the split must be three to one.
  4. Pick the odd one out. Do not let the sentence talk you out of it.

Worked example: one singular answer

Suppose the answers are:

  1. are restoring
  2. restore
  3. have restored
  4. restores

They are restoring, they restore, and they have restored all work. He restores works.

The split is three plural to one singular, so restores is correct.

content.prompt: Which answer is the singular odd one out?
content.hint: Try he before each complete answer. Only one will work.
content.explanation: Correct. He documents works. The other three choices fit after they.

blocks.html:
Worked example: one plural answer

The pattern can reverse:

  1. supports
  2. has supported
  3. is supporting
  4. support

The first three fit he. Only they support works.

The split is three singular to one plural, so support is correct.

content.prompt: Which answer is the plural odd one out?
content.hint: Three choices fit after he. Find the one that fits after they.
content.explanation: Yes. They influence works, while the other three choices fit after he.

blocks.html:
Once the gate passes, trust the pattern

A difficult SAT sentence may place several nouns near the blank. Those nouns are there to tempt you into matching the verb with the wrong word.

If the four choices pass the eligibility gate and produce a three-to-one split, you already have the answer.

Do not go hunting for the subject as a second check. That slower check can reintroduce the trap you just avoided.

content.prompt: This answer set passes the eligibility gate. Which choice is the odd one out?
content.hint: The first three fit after they. Which one fits after he?
content.explanation: Correct. Shapes is the singular odd one out. You did not need the sentence.

blocks.html:
The main danger: a tense or form question

Many SAT questions also place four verb forms in the answers but test tense, sequence, or sentence structure instead of singular versus plural.

The odd-one-out shortcut is likely to fail on those questions. That is why you must perform the eligibility test rather than merely noticing four verbs.

Stop when a choice fits both

A regular past-tense form often fits both testing frames:

  • he walked
  • they walked

Because walked is both singular and plural, the safety condition fails. Do not use the shortcut.

content.hint: Try both: he discovered; they discovered.
content.explanation: Right. Both frames work, so discovered is not exclusive. A choice like this blocks the shortcut.

blocks.html:
Stop when a choice fits neither

An -ing form by itself is not a complete verb:

  • he cataloging does not work
  • they cataloging does not work

That choice is neither singular nor plural. The safety condition fails, so do not use the shortcut.

A complete phrase such as is cataloging or are cataloging can still be classified normally.

content.prompt: Which choice is neither singular nor plural because it is not a complete verb by itself?
content.hint: Try placing each entire choice after both he and they.
content.explanation: Correct. Neither he recording nor they recording works. The standalone -ing form blocks the shortcut.

blocks.html:
Test the actual word—do not reject every past form

Was and were are past tense, but they still separate cleanly:

  • he was → singular
  • they were → plural

The rule is not “avoid past tense.” The rule is “every choice must fit exactly one testing frame.”

content.prompt: Which choice is the singular odd one out, making this set eligible for the shortcut?
content.hint: Try each complete choice after he and they. Three fit they; one fits he.
content.explanation: Correct. Was fits he; were, are, and have been fit they. Every choice fits exactly one frame, so the three-to-one set is eligible.

blocks.html:
A two-to-two split also fails

Suppose every choice fits exactly one frame, but two are singular and two are plural:

  1. is
  2. are
  3. has been
  4. have been

There is no single odd answer. Stop and solve the question using another verb strategy.

content.prompt: When is the odd-one-out shortcut safe?
choices: Whenever the four choices contain verbs, even if one of them fits both he and they.
Whenever at least one of the four choices ends in the letter -s.
Only when every choice is exclusively singular or plural and the split is three to one.
Only after you identify the complete subject of the sentence.
content.hint: Retrieve both parts of the gate: exclusive classification and one odd answer.
content.explanation: Correct. Every answer must fit one—and only one—of the testing frames, and exactly one answer must differ from the other three.

blocks.html:
Apply it to an SAT-style sentence

The collection of maps, together with several handwritten field journals, ___ how rapidly the coastline changed.

  1. have revealed
  2. reveal
  3. reveals
  4. are revealing

Do not analyze the sentence yet. Test the choices.

content.hint: Three choices fit after they. Find the one that fits after he.
content.explanation: Correct. Reveals is the singular odd one out. The nearby plural nouns never needed to enter your decision.

blocks.html:
Now reverse the pattern

New measurements of the distant stars, despite the limits of the original instruments, ___ the research team's conclusion.

  1. supports
  2. has supported
  3. is supporting
  4. support

content.hint: The first three fit after he. Which one fits only after they?
content.explanation: Right. Support is the plural odd one out, so it is correct.

blocks.html:
Recognize a question where the trick is unsafe

The laboratory ___ the samples last night.

  1. analyzed
  2. has analyzed
  3. will analyze
  4. analyzes

Several choices fit both he and they. This is not the odd-one-out subject–verb pattern.

content.prompt: What should you do with the laboratory question?
choices: Choose analyzes, because it is the one choice ending in -s.
Choose analyzed because past tense is always singular.
Use the odd-one-out trick after finding the nearest noun.
Do not use the shortcut; the choices are not exclusively singular or plural.
content.hint: Test analyzed and will analyze after both he and they.
content.explanation: Correct. He analyzed and they analyzed both work; so do he will analyze and they will analyze. The eligibility gate fails.

content.prompt: Which choice makes this answer set ineligible because it fits neither he nor they?
content.hint: Try each entire choice after both he and they. One choice cannot complete either frame.
content.explanation: Correct. Documenting alone is not a complete verb, so it fits neither frame and makes the set ineligible. Is documenting is a complete singular phrase.

blocks.html:
Independent transfer

The influence of the two architects, visible in the building's curved walls and open courtyards, ___ later designers throughout the region.

Run the complete process: scan, test, check the gate, and choose the odd one out.

content.hint: Classify every complete phrase with he and they. Three fit they; one fits he.
content.explanation: Correct. Has inspired is the singular odd one out. Once the three-to-one split appeared, the sentence could not distract you.

content.prompt: Which set should make you stop and use a different verb strategy?
choices: has changed; change; are changing; have changed
predicts; predict; are predicting; have predicted
content.hint: One set contains a choice that works after both he and they.
content.explanation: Right. Predicted fits both he and they, so that set fails the eligibility gate. Each of the other sets creates a clean three-to-one split.

content.prompt: A verb question with four choices. From memory: how do you run the odd-one-out test, and what has to be true before you're allowed to?
choices: Test every choice after he and they; continue only if the split is two to two; choose the answer that sounds correct after they.
Test every choice after the closest noun; continue only if each fits exactly one; choose the answer that matches the noun's number.
Test every choice after he and they; continue whenever at least one choice fits both; choose the answer that differs.
Test every choice after he and they; continue only if each fits exactly one and the split is three to one; choose the answer that differs.
content.hint: Retrieve the testing frames, the safety gate, and the final action.
content.explanation: You have it: he or they, exactly one, three to one, choose the different answer.

content.prompt: In 1911, a university expedition crossed the high plateau collecting alpine plants. The collection of field notebooks, sketches, and pressed specimens assembled by the expedition's two botanists ______ now housed in the university's herbarium, where conservators recently began digitizing it. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
content.hint: Run the frames: which choices fit after 'they,' and which fits after 'he'? Check the split.
content.explanation: Correct. The subject is the singular "collection" — the notebooks, sketches, specimens, and botanists are all inside interrupting phrases. In the frames, "is" fits "he" while "are," "were," and "have been" fit "they": a three-to-one split, so the odd one out wins.

content.html:
The odd one out — when the gate is open

He or they, three to one, done. If the four choices differ in tense instead of number, the gate is closed: read the sentence the long way.
